extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of travel/natural-history prose; naturalists and descriptive-writers seeking realistic field-based depiction
extracted.subtask_description: Producing accurate, scene-based travel and natural-history description grounded in first‑hand observation, seasonal/geographic specificity, and practical field methods; includes how to report findings and correct common traveller misconceptions. Useful for authors writing naturalist travelogues and descriptive essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate on‑the‑spot sketching / firsthand observation
rubrics_metrics.description: I have here given an accurate sketch of a luxuriant tropical scene as noted down on the spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize contemporaneous notes and direct observation when describing scenes; claim accuracy by recording impressions and details while present rather than relying on memory or second‑hand reports. Example: the author emphasizes that the sketch was noted on the spot to support its fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading aggregation of rare specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine tropical flowering-plants cultivated in our hothouses have been culled from the most varied regions, and therefore give a most erroneous idea of their abundance in any one region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create the impression that species or phenomena encountered across wide regions are abundant everywhere; avoid grouping together rare finds from different places as if they co‑occur in a single scene. Anti-pattern: describing a 'gay, flower-painted landscape' by aggregating scattered observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe individual scenes and their actual visual effect
rubrics_metrics.description: They have rarely studied and described individual scenes where vegetation was most luxuriant and beautiful, and fairly stated what effect was produced in them by flowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on specific locations and the actual effect observed there (colour, texture, absence/presence of flowers) rather than generalising. Give readers the scene's true character — e.g., foliage-dominated panoramas rather than imagined continuous floral display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground descriptions in seasonality and duration of residence
rubrics_metrics.description: A lengthened residence will show an abundance of magnificent and gaily-blossomed plants, but they have to be sought for...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report temporal context (season, month, wet/dry) and note how length of stay affects what is seen; long residence can reveal rarer phenomena but they may not be simultaneously present. Use temporal markers to qualify claims about abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise geographic and temporal markers
rubrics_metrics.description: By the beginning of December the regular wet season had set in... On December 13th I went on board a prau bound for the Aru Islands... I reached Menado on the 10th of June, 1859...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor narrative with dates, place names, and local seasonal conditions to orient the reader and support credibility. Specific dates and locations help readers evaluate claims and reproduce observations mentally or practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain causes and contextualise observations
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine tropical flowering-plants cultivated in our hothouses have been culled from the most varied regions... many of them are very rare, others extremely local...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide causal analysis when confronting expectations (why something is or isn't present). Contextual explanations (e.g., horticultural selection, habitat specificity) add depth and correct misconceptions rather than leaving observations as bare facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory, concrete detail and evocative similes
rubrics_metrics.description: They were somewhat musical too, having a deep vibrating note which at times closely resembles the tuning of two or three bass-viols in an orchestra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ auditory, visual, and tactile specifics and well‑chosen comparisons to familiar objects/instruments to make scenes vivid. Example: comparing frogs' notes to bass-viols conveys timbre and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast expectations with reality to correct clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader who is familiar with tropical nature only through the medium of books and botanical gardens will picture to himself many other natural beauties... But what is the reality? ... not one single spot of bright colour could be seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts between common tropes and your direct observations to challenge reader assumptions; explicitly state when popular or literary images differ from on‑site reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report field methods and collecting techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: I found that the rotten jack‑fruits were very attractive to many beetles, and used to split them partly open and lay them about in the forest... it was by spending half an hour at these when I had the time to spare, that I obtained the finest and most remarkable collection of this group of insects...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing natural-history or collection accounts, include practical methods (baiting, choice of microhabitats, timing of searches) so readers understand how specimens were obtained and the effort/technique behind discoveries. Examples given: splitting rotten fruit, searching damp pools, watching sugar‑palms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record observational micro‑locations and microhabitats
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost the only good place for them was in the dry beds of the streams in the forest, where, at damp places, muddy pools, or even on the dry rocks, all sorts of insects could be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the specific microhabitats where organisms are found (e.g., damp pools, rotten trunks, river beaches). Such specificity helps other collectors and enriches descriptive accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include social and quotidian detail to humanize description
rubrics_metrics.description: He usually rose before the sun, and after a cup of coffee looked after his servants, horses, and dogs, until seven, when a substantial breakfast... Putting on a clean white linen suit, he then drove to town...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend human routines, local customs, and character sketches (hosts' habits, village life) into natural description to situate nature within cultural life and give narrative variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative analogies to familiar climates for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: But it has been the custom of travellers to describe and group together all the fine plants they have met with during a long journey... the bright colours of flowers have a much greater influence on the general aspect of nature in temperate than in tropical climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare unfamiliar landscapes with temperate or well-known analogues to clarify differences, but do so carefully and with evidence; use comparison to illuminate rather than replace direct description.
